utterances.speaker: MS. IBRAHIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zikreta Ibrahimovic. I represent the attorney general of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NALCIOGLU

utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, as you all know, this is an application by the accused Ojdanic for the production of information and documents pursuant to Rule 54 bis. But before I move into the submissions, there are a few procedural matters that should be addressed. And first, is it Mr. Visnjic or Mr. Robinson who will be -- Mr. Robinson, yes. I just want to clarify the number of countries from whom you are now seeking binding orders. I will read the list which I have and you can correct me. And this would arise from the responses that have been received. Some progress would have been made. You are seeking orders from NATO, Belgium, Canada, the Czech Republic, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Iceland, Italy, Luxembourg, England, and the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. From the list of those who will make submissions today, there are two in respect of whom they are not seeking orders, Bosnia and Turkey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, in respect of Bosnia and Turkey, do I understand that you are not seeking orders from them and the application is withdrawn where they are concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We received on the 10th of February, 2003, a letter from the Republic of Turkey indicating they had no records responsive to our request. Similarly continue the 3rd of March, 2003, we received a letter from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina saying that they too had found no records responsive to our request. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I first ask the representative of Bosnia, representative of Bosnia -- and I have to apologise for this courtroom. It's not -- it has certain difficulties. But I can see the representative of Bosnia. You have heard what Mr. Robinson just said. Can you confirm that the position is the same, you have no information, no new information?

utterances.speaker: MS. IBRAHIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I confirm also that we do not have any new information about that, however, from the Chamber we received a summons to this hearing and we wanted to show cooperation with the ICTY. Now we have a changed situation, in so far as the security functions have been unified at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina and we have a ministry of justice at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Before coming to this hearing I consulted those two institutions, the ministry of justice of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the intelligence service of Bosnia and Herzegovina state, and they confirmed that they have not uncovered any new information or data. And this is -- and to that extent, the Defence's attitude and opinion holds. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, in particular for your spirit of cooperation. The representative of Turkey.

utterances.speaker: MR. NALCIOGLU
utterances.text: Mr. President, Turkey as a member of NATO country had troops in Kosovo, but after the incident -- not between the times of crimes, but our troops had been there after the incidents of the war crimes alleged by the Prosecutor. As a NATO country, we are here to cooperate if you have need, for justice. And if you have -- we have sent some documents produced by Turkey, but to be frank, we -- our troops had no intelligence capacity for interception on this point, because we have only a small troop that -- there is no special duty for interceptions. But if you do, members of the court or the counsel of the Mr. Ojdanic, we ask something on the case, we will be ready. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much for volunteering. In view of what Mr. Robinson has said, the Chamber does not require the presence of the representatives of Bosnia and Turkey, but if they wish to remain in the proceedings, they are perfectly free to do so. The next matter I want to deal with is an application from Canada, United States, and the Netherlands for in camera hearing. The Chamber has decided that it will proceed in public session until an issue of in camera hearing is raised. When it is raised, we will then deal with it. There is one other matter. That's the presence of the Prosecutor. Madam Prosecutor, an application had been made for the Prosecutor to be present during the --

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: As I was informed, the Defence counsel have nothing to oppose about our presence here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is no objection from the accused? Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We would like them to be here and have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Johnson for the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We, too, have no objection to the Prosecution in this hearing, but if you wouldn't mind going back to the previous matter we did have some additional thoughts and reasons why we would request that this hearing be conducted in closed session. If Your Honours would permit, I would like to briefly some of those additional matters for your consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you do that, may I just say that the Prosecutor can be present.

utterances.speaker: MS. DEL PONTE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. As you indicated on Friday, the United States, Canada, and the Netherlands submitted written requests for the proceedings to be conducted in closed session. Since that time, the United Kingdom, Germany, France and Turkey have indicated to us that they too support this request, and therefore my presentation to you is on behalf of all of the NATO countries participating in this hearing. We believe that Your Honours should grant our request that the session proceed in closed proceedings for the following reasons. First, Rule 54 bis itself provides for states to make such a request and for it to be granted by the Chamber when there is prejudice to national security interest. In this particular case the heart of the Defence application that is before you relates not just to intelligence information but also to the sources and methods for producing it. That is at the core of what they are requesting. All of the written submissions that you have before you have indicated that the requested information would prejudice the national security interests of the participating countries and have objected on that on bases. The Defence itself in its application acknowledges that: "The nature of this information sought by this request impacts on national security." Indeed, the declaration they submitted earlier in November was a detailed analysis of information sources and methods. So to our mind it is inevitable that the discussion of this application will touch and will touch repeatedly on intelligence information, intelligence sources and methods which are of the most sensitive national security concern. Now, the request that we have before you for reconsideration is a narrow one. Although the rules provide that we could request additional protective measures, such as that this hearing be conducted ex parte, without the presence of the Defence, or that a transcript not be made, we're not requesting that. We believe that our interests can be protected if the session itself is conducted in closed session and participation is limited to the Prosecution, the participating states, and court personnel. I would also like to briefly touch on a couple of the matters that were raised by counsel for the Defence in their -- in the written opposition they submitted. The Defence, for example, noted that our pleadings were in public. And while that is true, the public pleadings were reviewed carefully before they were submitted to ensure that national security interests were protected. But in this proceeding we expect these issues to be discussed in additional detail. Moreover, we can't predict now what Your Honours or the Defence will ask us and which areas will be explored in relation to these proceedings. What we do know is that they involve an application that centres on intelligence to an extraordinary degree. We also do not think it is conducive to the efficient conduct of the proceedings for us to move repeatedly between open and closed sessions. First, we think that would be disruptive to our presentations to the Court; but secondly, the fact that we would at particular instances signal a desire to go into closed session would in and of itself flag an area of heightened national security concern. We think that our proposal strikes a sensible balance between these competing equities so we can have a detailed and efficient hearing on this matter with the participation of the Defence in a manner that's protective of our national security interests. So we would therefore request, Your Honours, to please reconsider our request on behalf of the participating NATO countries. And I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Johnson. Mr. Robinson, in response.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We strongly oppose the hearing in closed session. We think this is a matter of great public interest. Rule 54 bis (F) is permissive, it's not mandatory. It says it may be closed. I suggest that that particular rule deals with a session in which the Judges are dealing with particular documents in which there's a need for a closed session. I can assure you that I can make my entire presentation today without any reference to any sensitive matters of national security, since I know no sensitive information about any country's national security. I think the best way to proceed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So you don't agree, then, with the submission that security concerns are so pervasive in this application that it would not be efficient of proceedings, because we would be going in and out from public to private session repeatedly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can't speak for what the others may say at this hearing, but I know from our presentation there's absolutely no reason to go into private or closed session. But if, for example, during the presentation of the United States they wish to raise something that they feel is sensitive, they can make an application at that time with respect to that portion of the hearing. But to close the entire hearing to the public would be like killing an ant with an elephant gun. It's not necessary and it's not within the practice of the Tribunal with respect to having open and closed proceedings. They should be narrowly tailored to protect the interests that need to be protected, and that can be done when the party seeking closed session when there's something particularly sensitive to be said. We wouldn't object at that point if such a showing was made. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll consider that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In considering this matter we have to balance the accused's right of public hearing against the legitimate concerns of the states of their national security. We believe that certainly Mr. Robinson has indicated that in his address he will not have any matters touching upon national security such as would require us to go into a closed session. So as far as he's concerned, he can -- his submissions can be in open session. When we come to consider the arguments raised by the United States, there are proper concerns; but we believe they can be addressed by identifying them when they arise, and that is what we will do. But if in the course of the proceedings matters reach a stage where it becomes inefficient to continue moving from public to private session repeatedly, then we'll consider going into closed session for the rest of the proceedings. But at this stage, we'll begin in open session. Mr. Robinson will make his presentation in open session. And the states will make their presentations in open session, subject to the exception that I have identified. We begin then with the applicant, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, members of the Trial Chamber. I'll just take a moment to give myself a proper introduction. I am Peter Robinson. I am privileged to be counsel for General Ojdanic here at the ICTY, along with my colleagues. I am a proud citizen of the United States of America, member of the bar, and resident of California. I would like to thank the states for their participation in General Ojdanic’s request. I appreciate all the effort that has gone into dealing with this request, and I hope that these proceedings can result in a constructive discussion that will end in a resolution consistent with both General Ojdanic's right to a fair trial and the resources and secrets of the states. What we've requested is three sorts of information: First, intercepted conversations in which General Ojdanic is a party, between Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the 1st of January and the 20th of June 1999; the second, intercepted conversations in which General Ojdanic is mentioned, again between the 1st of January and the 20th of June, 1999, which is the period of the events charged in the indictment; also with the limitation that the conversation originate in the Republic of Yugoslavia and also with the limitation that it contained the topic of Kosovo. Our third request are statements by General Ojdanic to representatives of the states or persons working on their behalf, again limited to the period covered by the events in the indictment, 1st of January to the 20th of June, 1999. It's an extraordinary request by an accused. To my knowledge, it's the first time at any Tribunal that an accused has requested and has been willing to have public disclosure of his unguarded, private conversations. The reason for the application is simple. General Ojdanic is not guilty. He never planned, instigated, ordered, committed, or otherwise aided and abetted any war crimes. He had no knowledge of any plan to deport Albanians from Kosovo, and he never joined any criminal enterprise to do so. And as a commander, his standing orders, from which he never varied, were that war crimes were to be prevented and punished. We need this evidence that we're seeking in this proceedings today to prove that. While the request from the accused is extraordinary, there are already in place well-established legal principles at this Tribunal to deal with it. We have provisions in our Statute, our Rules, two decisions from the Appeals Chamber, and decisions from this Trial Chamber in the Milosevic case relating to Serbia and Montenegro. So we're not asking you to make new law; we're asking you to fairly apply existing principles. Article 29 of Statute provides that "states shall comply without undue delay with any request for assistance or an order issued by a Trial Chamber, including but not limited to the taking of testimony and production of evidence." This was part of Resolution 827 unanimously adopted by the Security Council including the United States, United Kingdom, and France. In the comments of the Kingdom of the Netherlands at the time of the adoption of Article 29, they said Chapter 7 of the United Nations Charter "provides the necessary basis to ensure in every way that states cooperate with every possible way with the investigation and prosecution of war crimes in the former Yugoslavia." In the Appeals Chamber decision in the Blaskic case, Article 29's provisions were held to be valid and mandatory. So we are invoking Article 29 in the orders we seek today. We know that NATO and four countries have not responded at all to the request, those countries being Belgium, Iceland, Luxembourg and Poland. It's our position that regardless of the outcome of these proceedings, An order should be submitted to them, because they have waived their objections both by not being present here and by not responding in writing to the Trial Chamber's orders. With respect to Article 29 those that have appeared here are seeking to be classified in some cases as concerned bystanders, but the Blaskic appeals decision makes it clear that Article 29 applies to all countries. The Appeals Chamber said that it should again be emphasised that the plain wording of Article 29 makes it clear that the obligation it creates is incumbent upon all member states, irrespective of whether or not they are states of the former Yugoslavia. The Government of Canada says that it's a bystander, not implicated in the activity under investigation, and therefore it should not be subject to the terms of Article 29. That same argument is made by the Kingdom of Netherlands and the United Kingdom. First I would point out if someone were to take a walk around downtown Belgrade and see what was the Ministry of Defence or take a look at the Chinese embassy one would see the damage done by these so-called bystanders to this conflict. The Government of Canada and all the NATO members were not bystanders, they were belligerents. And the Blaskic opinion says that as former belligerents parties they are more likely hold important evidence needed by the Tribunal. The Government of the United Kingdom seems to indicate that because it made the most strenuous efforts to prevent the offences charged in the indictment, it somehow should be exempted from having to disclose materials pursuant to Article 29. And I would cite the Trial Chamber to the Todorovic decision, in which you, Judge Robinson, participated in involving SFOR when all they did was arrest him, but they were required to provide records about that arrest. And they were not exempted from Article 29. And no country here should be so exempted. We'll also governed by Rule 54 bis of the rules, which provides that "a party requesting an order under Rule 54 that a state produce documents or information shall apply in writing to the relevant Judge or Trial Chamber and shall meet three criteria: one, to identify as far as possible the documents or information to which the application relates; two, to indicate how they are relevant to any matter in issue before the Judge or Trial Chamber and necessary for a fair determination of that matter; and three, to explain the steps that have been taken by the applicant to secure the state's assistance." I note that the Trial Chamber has already made a preliminary finding with respect to each of these matters. I'd like to discuss them very briefly. First, with respect to the question of specificity. In a Scheduling Order of the 22nd of November, 2002, the Trial Chamber said: "Considering that the applicant has met the requirements of Rule 54 bis (A) in that the applicant has satisfied the Trial Chamber as far as possible the documents or information to which the application relates." We're guided on the issue of specificity by the Blaskic decision which says that documents should be identified as far as possible and in addition be limited in number. And the Kordic appeals decision was probably the most direct on point with respect to the specificity requirement. It says that "the underlying purpose of the requirement of specificity is to allow a state to be able to identify the requested documents for the purpose of turning them over to the requesting party. The requirement of specificity clearly prohibits the use of broad categories, but does not prohibit the of categories as such. A requested category of documents has to be defined with sufficient clarity to enable ready identification of documents falling within that category." The Kordic Appeals Chamber said that that doesn't exclude all requests that involve the production of hundreds of documents because considering the nature of the complex charges heard by the Tribunal it's hard to see how that can be avoided. Consequently, the critical question is whether the obligation falling upon the state is unduly onerous, taking into account whether the difficulty of producing the evidence is not disproportionate to the extent that the process is strictly justified by the exigencies of the trial. And indeed, in the Milosevic's decisions with respect to Serbia and Montenegro, this Trial Chamber has ordered production of categories of documents including minutes of meetings of bodies covering up to a seven-year period. We note that the standard of ready -- whether there can be ready identification of documents sought has apparently been met by a number of countries that have responded to our request. We node that Bosnia, Turkey, Norway, Portugal, Albania, Denmark, Macedonia, Romania, Spain and Croatia have been able to conduct searches of their records within the criteria given, and in fact Croatia has produced documents, intercepted conversations, pursuant to our request. With respect to specificity, we took the extra step of consulting with an expert Witness, James Bamford and we got a declaration from him to assist the Trial Chamber. And in that declaration he describes in detail the process, to his knowledge, that would have to be undertaken to obtain the records and his opinion that the records as we've described them are not unduly onerous to be produced, at least with the United States, the country with which he's familiar. I would note that in the United States we have what's called the Privacy Act, which is found at Title 5 of the United States Code, Section 552 (A). And this act says that "any citizen of the United States by submitting his name and date of birth to an agency of the government can have the government produce for him all of the records in its possession which relate to that person." And so the United States, at least, has the capacity to search by name to locate all of the records relating to that person. And indeed it does so as a matter of regular course and has been doing so for many years. So we believe the requested categories that we've set out adequately allow the states to make ready identification of the documents that we're seeking. Now, how do we know that they have useful information? Canada says that our request is based on mere speculation that the states might have something of value to us. Well, first we have the declaration of the expert James Bamford who said that interceptions by the United States and United Kingdom which have included those of General Ojdanic, given his position, and giving communications involving an army chief of a country of which the United States was at war would likely be retained. Media reports, including those in the New York Times reported that the arsenal of modern spying, satellites and drones that hovered in the sky during the Kosovo conflict has yielded reams of material. There are intercepts of telephone and radio conversations between commanders in the field, and that's quoted at our motion on paragraph 4. And the Washington Post, with respect to the Racak incident, indicated that the orders came by Serb-led Belgrade government, according to telephone intercepts by Western governments. And the information which was quoted from those alleged telephone intercepts was said to have been leaked to the news media by Western sources familiar with the intercepts. In Newsweek, Miroslav Tudjman, the son of the late president of Croatia, said that the American CIA spent at least $10 million on Croatian listening posts, to intercept telephone calls in Bosnia and Croatia. Indeed, the Bosnian government did turn over intercepts, including telephone conversations of General Ojdanic, conversations about General Ojdanic in which others were speaking. And those conversations, for example, show General Ojdanic's relationship with President Milosevic; his genuine concern for eight soldiers who happen to have been kidnapped by the KLA at the time; his efforts to find a peaceful solution to that situation; to the fact that in his conversations that were intercepted there was no mention of expelling ethnic Albanians or retaliations for the war crimes in retaliation for the kidnapping of these soldiers. The conversation between President Milosevic and Milutinovic also shows that he was directed to act in a proper way without war crimes being committed. We also know by reading the book written by General Wesley Clark that he had several conversations with General Ojdanic, and that comes within Category C of which we're seeking by this order. And in an article written by a fellow who used to be the coordinator of war crimes in Kosovo between the United Kingdom and the ICTY, David Gowin, published in the 13th volume of the International Journal of the International Law at page 913, he says: "The United Kingdom broke new ground in the provision of intelligence information in Kosovo to the Office of the Prosecutor and that provided information about the actions and decisions of the FRY government and actions, deployment, composition, and practices of the FRY police, army, and paramilitary forces." So we have a good basis for believing that if the orders that were requested were issued, valuable information will be disclosed that will be relevant to the trial. We don't say that we have the magic words for describing the records that we're seeking. We've done our best. I have to say that the responses of the states have failed to suggest any workable modifications to our requests. Canada has suggested that the requests should be narrowed to only those conversations showing whether General Ojdanic participated in crimes or in a joint criminal enterprise; whether war crimes were reported to him; his state of mind; and the prevention and punishment of war crimes. The Netherlands has suggested that disclosure should be limited to those conversations which have a bearing on General Ojdanic's participation in, knowledge of, or state of mind concerning the crimes alleged. We suggest that these criteria are too subjective to be practical. It's the Trial Chamber or the Defence who's in the best position to know whether a conversation bears upon these issues. For example, in the Croatian intercepts we've received, even innocuous references made to someone unfamiliar with the case may not appear to have any bearing on any of these issues can well be highly relevant to the issues before the Trial Chamber in this trial. In addition, even innocuous statements may be useful in establishing General Ojdanic's presence in a particular place or his occupation with other tasks at a particular time. The Netherlands and the United Kingdom and the United States have also suggested that General Ojdanic should be required to specify the communications and statements that he would like copies of. I would ask you to think for a minute if you can remember all the people you talked to between January 1 and June 20th 1999. I know General Ojdanic can't. And there are no records that would be complete enough to be able to allow him to reconstruct such a thing. So there's no way in which we can provide to the states some kind of lists of everyone he spoke to during that six-month period. Nor can he be expected to recall the substance of those conversations. And so we would respectfully submit and we're open to -- looking forward to listening to suggestions here and over the next day or two, but we've yet to hear any practical details on why the states cannot retrieve the material sought by General Ojdanic as framed and what constructive improvements can be made if necessary to those requests. The second criteria under Rule 54 bis is that of relevance. And I can be brief on this. You've made a preliminary finding of relevance in your order of 22 November 2002. And the Appeals Chamber in Kordic has been very clear, the state from which documents are requested does not have the locus standi to challenge their relevance. So I will say no more about relevance. I don't believe that any of the states should be addressing the issue of relevance, but if the Trial Chamber has any questions about relevance, either now or at the conclusion of the proceedings, I would be happy to address that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, is that what that statement means? Did it mean that the question of relevance is ultimately a matter for the Trial Chamber? It's not a matter to be determined by the requesting state. It doesn't mean that that state can't raise it. It can raise it but it can't determine it; that's a matter for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Respectfully, Mr. President, I disagree. It says the state from which the documents are requested does not have the locus standi to challenge their relevance. Challenge. That's because the states are not in a position to know the relevance. That's between the Prosecution and the Defence. The Prosecution can probably challenge the relevance of documents that are being sought by the Defence from a third party, if it had an inclination to do so. But the states do not have under the Kordic case, at least the way I read it, it's none of their business basically as to whether something is relevant or not. That's between the parties to a litigation. Certainly the Trial Chamber on its own can raise the issue of relevance and indeed has to decide it. So I'm happy to discuss it if it's something you want to hear. But it's our position that under the Kordic appeals decision it's not a proper subject for this hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you direct me to the paragraph in Kordic where that's dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's at paragraph 40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll turn now to the third prong of the test under Rule 54 bis, and that is our efforts to obtain the material from the states prior to seeking a binding order. Again, in your order of the 22nd of November, you found that our steps that we had taken were adequate. We believe that was a correct finding. On the 15th of May, 2002 -- actually less than a month after General Ojdanic voluntarily surrendered to this Tribunal, we sent a letter to all of the states and we asked them to voluntary submit material which we described in three requests. The requests cover the same information that is pending before the Trial Chamber, but we narrowed them. And the reason we did that is we discussed with states who responded to our letter their concerns and we tried to take those into account and do the best we could to make the requests as narrow as possible to still accomplish what we felt needed to be accomplished. And that's the result of our application in November 2002. We had intended to file our application within 30 days of sending the letters to the states, but we delayed for six months while we met with the United States and communicated with the other states. We ultimately narrowed our requests based on their objections. When we filed our motion on the 13th of November, 2002, we also served it on all the states directly and invited them to contact us to try to arrange for some satisfactory resolution. It's now been two years. We've never received any documents and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. from the responses from the states that are here, I think we can see they are unwilling to provide the material we seek, whether by informal request or formal motion. So we believe that we've satisfied the third criteria under Rule 54 bis. Now, there also arises the question whether states have the right to refuse to provide information on national security grounds. And the answer to that question is a clear no, and that is provided by the Blaskic's appeals decision. The Appeals Chamber said: "To allow national security considerations to prevent the International Tribunal from obtaining documents that might prove of decisive importance to the conduct of trials would be tantamount to undermining the very essence of the International Tribunal's functions. To grant states a blanket right to withhold for security purposes documents necessary for trial might jeopardise the very function of the International Tribunal and defeat its essential object and purpose." Now, the United States on February 28th of 2003 made a submission that the disclosure of intercepted conversations -- indeed, even confirmation that it does or does not exist would cause great harm to the national security interests of the United States. I would now like to play for the Trial Chamber about 80 seconds of a video of Secretary of State Colin Powell addressing the Security Council of the United States just earlier than that, that bear on the question of intercepted conversations. May that now be played, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: COLIN POWELL: Mr. President, Mr. Secretary-General, distinguished colleagues, I would like to begin by expressing my thanks for the special effort that each of you made to be here today. This is an important day for us all as we review the situation with respect to Iraq and its disarmament obligations under UN Security Council Resolution 1441.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're going to play two other portions immediately thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: COLIN POWELL: ... international community. Indeed the facts and Iraq's behaviour -- "Mr. President, Mr. Secretary-General, distinguished colleagues, I would like to begin by expressing my thanks for the special effort that each of you made to be here today. This is an important day for us all as we review the situation with respect to Iraq and its disarmament obligations under UN Security Council Resolution 1441 -- "-- made no effort to disarm as required by the international community. Indeed, the facts and Iraq's behaviour show that Saddam Hussein and his regime are concealing their efforts to produce more weapons of mass destruction. Let me begin by playing a tape for you. What you are about to hear is a conversation that my government monitored. It takes place on November 26th of last year, on the day before United Nations teams resumed inspections in Iraq. The conversation involves two senior officers, a colonel and a brigadier general from Iraq's elite military unit, the Republican Guard. 'On January 20th, four days later, Iraq promised the inspectors it would search for more. You will now hear an officer from Republican Guard headquarters issuing an instruction to an officer in the field. Their conversation took place just last week, on January 30th.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, while the United States was representing to this Tribunal that the mere conversation of -- that intercepted conversations does or did not exist would cause grave harm to the national security interests of the United States, they were at the same time playing for the public intercepted conversations that had been intercepted only one week earlier in Iraq. So it's clear that there has to be some incentive to make this in the United States' national interest to have these conversations disclosed. And I suggest to you that such an incentive must come from this Trial Chamber under Rule 54 bis because the representations that were made to you by the United States show that they simply don't want to discuss or disclose intercepted conversations in this forum because it doesn't suit them, but in the United Nations when they're trying to get the other countries to invade Iraq and when it does suit them, they're willing to disclose intercepted conversations, even as fresh as one week old.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, just go back to the passage that you've cited from Blaskic. I don't put the interpretation on it that you have. I see it as saying nothing more than that state does not have a blanket right to refuse to disclose information on the basis of national security concerns. And Blaskic was before Rule 54 bis. Now, Rule 54 bis sets out a regime to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I actually agree with you, and I am about to discuss, in my opinion, at least the fact that Rule 54 bis decided that the national security interests of the states should be dealt with by the modalities that it set forth in Rule 54 bis (F) and 54 bis (G), so it doesn't give the state the right to withhold national security information. What it does it sets up a mechanism for protection of that information from disclosure. But it's the Trial Chamber or the Judge who decides whether that information is disclosed or not disclosed on a national security basis, not the country itself. The obligation to provide the documents still exists and cannot be avoided by raising national security concerns. But when such concerns are raised, there are modalities to deal with that. They can produce the documents, they can do it in camera. They can be done ex parte. They can do it with one Judge. They can have their own translations. There doesn't have to be a transcript. They can provide them redacted. They can have a signed affidavit in lieu of some documents and the documents can be returned to them, those decided by the Trial Chamber not to be disclosed. Those are all the protections set forth in Rules 54 bis (F) and (G). But that's how we deal with at this Tribunal national security, not by allowing the states to escape their obligations to provide them, but to protect them in the confines of this Tribunal so they can be properly disclosed with the balance of the rights of the accused and the rights of the states. The Government of Canada has said that the process of disclosing and examining sensitive information set forth in Rules 54 bis (F) and (G) should not be engaged in where the state has made a compelling case of prejudice regarding national security interests, has a history of cooperation with the Tribunal, and is a bystander. I suggest to you that's not the law. First of all, they're not bystander. They do have a history of cooperation with the Tribunal. It doesn't give them any special treatment in the question of whether or not they have to provide these records. Certainly, the bona fides of their representations in this Tribunal ought to be given great weight, but it doesn't excuse them from their obligations under Rule 54 bis or Article 29. The Netherlands says that the disclosure of intercepted conversations and human intelligence could jeopardise the methods used to generate such information. As you've seen on the video, it's common knowledge that conversations are intercepted by governments, especially in times of war. In conclusion, I would like to go back to the remarks that Madeleine Albright made --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you do that. You've skipped over relevance very quickly for reasons you've explained, but that particular part of the rule implies that not only the material sought should be relevant but necessary for a fair determination of that issue. So even assuming you are right about the Appeals Chamber's intention in making the statement which you drew on in Blaskic, there still is a question of necessity to be addressed and your calls for material in this case are extremely wide. And indeed, if you take the first one as an example, it doesn't even indicate that it relates to issues in the trial at all. It's not confined to issues in the trial. It would cover any conversation of any type that General Ojdanic had during the period in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. And there is a reason for that and perhaps this would be a good opportunity for me to give you those reasons. It's our belief that this disclosure is necessary for a fair determination of this case, because it will show that General Ojdanic did not participate in any of the crimes charged in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. I mean, I do follow that argument, but what I don't follow at the moment is why you don't even give us a few examples of circumstances which he's bound to be able to remember during that period where you can show to us something to confirm it might be necessary in the context of a case where perhaps there's going to be a circumstantial case set against him and you're anxious to secure circumstances to back up his potential evidence in the trial itself. But none of that is presented in your application.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can give you some examples and I don't think necessarily I want to be limited to these examples, but I'll give you one: For example, when General Ojdanic learned of the incident in Racak in January of 1999, he had communications the subordinates and asked them to investigate and find out what went on in Racak and what was the involvement of the Yugoslavian army in that incident. And later, he had communications from subordinates in which he was told that the army was not involved. That's one example of the types of communications that would be relevant to the trial. I think that the reason we haven't limited our request to specific incidents is because there's other things that are impossible to predict that may very well relate to General Ojdanic's state of mind. Many other conversations he could have with subordinates, with President Milosevic, with other people can reflect upon his state of mind without necessarily being even identifiable as discussing any particular incident that's in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But, Mr. Robinson, it's not necessary for an application of this nature to cover every possible eventuality. There are certain obligations upon the applicant. It may be that that could result in the recovery of certain material because you've identified it sufficiently well to show that it's -- you've specified what it is and that it's necessary for the Defence. That may lead to a further application, for example. But what you're asking for here requires, speaking for myself, very strong justification in view of the width of the calls themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. I think that as a practical matter, even from the declaration that you see from our expert, these records are stored and are searchable in electronic form, and the most common way to search for data in an electronic form is by a word search. And by searching for the word "Ojdanic" you at least can get a body of data that is then relevant, at least potentially relevant. Then you can limit that data further; the period of time of the indictment, limit that further. Now you have a smaller body of data. Now the question is: Who should be looking at this material to determine whether or not it deals with the state of mind of General Ojdanic or deals with his role in the command structure of Yugoslavia, and all these other things. We want at least the Trial Chamber to be making that -- looking at those records to make those determinations, not someone sitting in a room in some nation's capital who doesn't know anything about the case. Because we're likely to have a body of materials which may not be evident to the average person as being relevant or even exculpatory but in fact could be highly useful to your determination of the facts in this case. So we haven't been able to think of a way to narrow our request any further and yet get the kind of material that we're looking for. Secondly, the negative evidence from receiving documents responsive to this request is also very important for the Trial Chamber to consider. To show that although contemporaneous recordings of a specified number of General Ojdanic's conversations were obtained and reviewed, that General Ojdanic was never heard to say anything that would indicate that he had knowledge of, participated in, planned or condoned any of the crimes charged in the indictment, that is also a powerful piece of evidence for the Trial Chamber to consider. So by having the country's collect -- pool the relevant information and have it submitted to the Trial Chamber or to the Defence, we would then be in a position to make that representation and for you to have confidence in it. It's an important point in your determination of whether or not General Ojdanic committed the offences for which he's charged. So while ideally to narrow this request as much as possible is the goal, you can't narrow it to the point where things escape that would be relevant and useful. We've done our best to try to balance this dilemma of trying not create too much work for the states but create a pool of useful information for the Trial Chamber and for General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I would just like to conclude now with remarks that were made by Ambassador Madeleine Albright at the adoption of the Resolution creating this Tribunal. She said: "This will be no victor's Tribunal. The only victor that will prevail in this endeavour is the truth." I would ask the Trial Chamber and all the parties involved in these hearings to spend the next few days, to strive to meet that goal to provide information that will allow you to determine the truth in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, doesn't your inability to narrow the application any further mean that you're essentially fishing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I think that you can say that any application is fishing, including applications that you've approved in the Milosevic case. For example, to ask for all the minutes of the meetings of the Supreme Defence Council of Yugoslavia; one could say that that is fishing. But nevertheless the request is narrow enough to think that you're fishing in a relatively limited pond and there's a lot of fish underneath. That's the goal. I think any application can be said to be fishing, but the goal is to narrow your pond and to have as many fish as possible in that pond. I think we have done that and that's why I think the application should be granted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We are scheduled to take a break -- in fact, should have taken a break at 4.o’clock. We'll now break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll now hear submissions on behalf of Canada from Ms. Swords.

utterances.speaker: MS. SWORDS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Members of the Tribunal, it's an honour to appear before you today on behalf of the Government of Canada. Canada welcomes this opportunity to appear before the Tribunal, as we are greatly concerned with the precedent-setting implications of the order sought by the applicant. Our submissions today focus primarily on how this application fails to meet the requirements of Rule 54 bis, and thereby undermines the efficient and fair process that is the purpose of that rule. These points were covered in some detail in our written submission of February 27th, 2003, which we continued to rely on. Today we will briefly highlight some aspects of that submission, in light of the applicant's further submission on relevance filed in June 2003, and his statement here today. We will submit that the application should be dismissed. We will also, as a final and practical matter, underline that the very broad nature of the applicant's request makes it extremely difficult for the parties to engage meaningfully and in good faith in the process of voluntary cooperation that is envisaged by Rule 54 bis. I turn first to our most fundamental concern with the application: that it is plainly inconsistent with the overall purpose and scheme of Rule 54 bis. Nothing in the applicant's further submission on relevance, which was filed in June 2003, responded to this concern. As a result, our objections to the application as identified in our written submission remain unanswered. As pointed out in our written submission, the Tribunal has held in the Blaskic subpoena decision that the Tribunal's powers of compulsion must be applied with restraint and circumspection vis-a-vis states who are, after all, not direct parties to prosecutions before the Tribunal. That is at paragraph 31 of the decision. As a preliminary observation, therefore, Canada respectfully submits that the Tribunal must continue to be wary of attempts to misuse the potent provisions of Rule 54 bis. Our concern over noncompliance with Rule 54 bis in this case stems from the fact that virtually none of the rule's requirements are met by the defendant's application. In particular, the application has two main problems. It is a classic fishing expedition and it seeks irrelevant and unnecessary information. In addition, it needlessly raises national security concerns. Let me touch very briefly upon these problematic features of the application. Turning first to the fishing expedition argument. The applicant establishes no basis for believing that Canada has particular information Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that would be relevant and necessary to his defence, as he must according to Rule 54 bis and the related jurisprudence of this Tribunal. As Judge Hunt said in the Appeals Chamber decision in Delalic - it's at paragraph 4 of the decision and we cite it in our submission at paragraph 8, and I quote: "A party is not entitled to have an order made to produce material so that he may have access to it simply because he says that the material is irrelevant [sic] to an issue in the trial or appeal. He is not entitled to conduct a fishing expedition in the sense that he wishes to inspect the material in order to discover whether he has any case at all to make. An order to produce is not the same as obtaining discovery against a party." The applicant should be able to identify the particular information that he believes to be crucial to his defence and to explain how it is crucial. Unlike the Prosecutor, states are not subject to disclosure obligations. So to expect the state to respond to what amounts to a sweeping request for disclosure rather than for a request for production of identified information is unreasonable, excessive, and falls outside the scope of Rule 54 bis. In other words, the applicant is engaged in a classic fishing expedition: asking for extremely broad classes of information without having first established any basis for his belief that Canada has anything of relevance. And the applicant's further submission of June 2003 does nothing to narrow the scope of his request or explain its basis. The applicant must narrow his request to that which is relevant and necessary. If he is unable to do so, one may infer that in fact he does not know where the relevant information exists, and thus that his request is indeed a speculative and massive fishing expedition, exactly what the Rules and jurisprudence are designed to preclude. As for the requirements of relevance a necessity, the applicant has not shown the relevance of most of the information he seeks. His request is extremely broad. For example, as presently formulated, the Defence application seeks, among other things, all communications during a six-month period to which General Ojdanic was a party. This would capture virtually anything, including, for example, telephone calls in which the applicant made arrangements for social arrangements, as Judge Bonomy has eluded to. Obviously not everything can be relevant to his defence. So the application is clearly not tailored to capture only relevant and necessary documents. Again, the application falls outside the scope of Rule 54 bis. The applicant submitted today that the relevance of requested information is none of their business, referring to the states here today. The support for that proposition is a Court decision at paragraph 40, but that decision predates Rule 54 bis. Rule 54 bis expressly in paragraph (A) makes the request of information from states a central issue. And I would recall that Rule 54 bis is specifically meant to address applications for production directed at states. It is therefore obvious that states are entitled to address issues of relevance in responding to applications for production orders, particularly those that are so extensive as the one before us today. Now, in his supplementary submission of June 2003, the applicant tries to justify his extremely broad request by explaining that he wants to prove a negative. For example, at page 4, paragraph 9 of his further submission, the applicant submits that intercepts of his communications would allow him to show that he had no culpable knowledge of events in Kosovo, and I quote: "By showing in the aggregate that despite being intercepted on X number of calls during the very time period that the crimes were alleged to have taken place, he was never heard to order, plan instigate, aid and abet, condone or fail to prevent or punish a war crime." And again at page 5, paragraph 13 of his further submission the applicant says that disclosure of his contemporaneous statements will provide evidence that: "In the aggregate with the interception of X number of calls concerning General Ojdanic, there was no evidence upon which it could be concluded that he participated in, had knowledge of, condoned, or failed to punish a war crime." In other words, the applicant is simply not interested in any exculpatory evidence states may have; rather, he wants to rely on what states do not have to try to establish his innocence by negative inference. There are at least two problems with this. First, such a an approach would require numerous states to offer up enormous amounts of information so the applicant can sift through it all in the hopes of finding nothing relevant. This is not what Rule 54 bis provides for. The Tribunal held in the Blaskic decision at paragraph 32 that an applicant must: "Identify specific documents and not broad categories." And again: "A party cannot request hundreds of documents." The further problem with this approach is that it is absolutely unnecessary. The proposed approach confuses the burden of proof in a criminal trial. The Defence need not have access to large portions of the archival holdings of now 15 states in order to show that they hold nothing incriminating, and thus that he must be presumed innocent. Rather, it's for the Prosecutor to introduce positive evidence of his guilt. Failure by the Prosecutor to produce the necessary incriminating evidence permits - indeed compels - the drawing of the relevance inference as to innocence. It is neither necessary nor relevant for the accused to raise a presumption of innocence by claiming that he has been unable to find anything incriminating. Clearly, the order proposed by the applicant falls outside the scope of Rule 54 bis. To use the words of Rule 54 bis (B) itself, the application should be rejected by the Trial Chamber because the: "Documents or information are not relevant to any matter in issue in the proceedings before them or are not necessary for a fair determination of any such matter." Mr. President and members of the Tribunal, in any event Canada objects to the application on the grounds that as currently worded it would prejudice Canada's national security interests. Canada's position on national security is set out in some detail in our written submission, and I will not repeat it here. What I do want to underline is that the applicant's request is specifically framed in such a way so as to target the most sensitive forms or sources of information, such as communication intercepts. In seeking sensitive information from a state, a party should resort to means that are the least prejudicial to the national security interests of the state. So the applicant should be focusing on relevant informational content, rather than its sources or means of collection. And he has done just the opposite here. As a final and more practical matter, this application is not a genuine measure of last resort, which it must be before the order sought would be justified. Canada respects its obligations under the Statute and Rules to act in good faith in responding to requests for assistance. But a party seeking assistance must also act in accordance with the Statute and Rules in good faith. This means, in part, that a compulsory order should only be sought when all voluntary avenues of cooperation have been exhausted. This is inherent in Rule 54 bis and essential to the fair and efficient functioning of this Tribunal. But pursuing voluntary avenues of cooperation requires more than an unfocused and speculated request followed by an application for compulsory measures. What is required is that a requesting state exhaust all avenues of cooperation. That is, a requesting party must respect the parameters and spirit of the Statute and the Rules by making appropriate, reasonable, and relevant requests. Failing to do so undermines any real possibility of voluntary cooperation. Indeed, despite the very general nature of this request, we began doing some preliminary searching and we soon realised that without some specificity we could not properly assess what information might be relevant and necessary for the Defence. Nor should we be required to do so. It is the applicant who must narrow the field to what is actually relevant and necessary to his defence. He is the one who must make voluntary cooperation possible by making a reasonable request. He must, in other words, make good-faith efforts to give voluntary cooperation a true chance. In that spirit, we remain prepared to work with counsel for the applicant and to discuss with them reasonable requests for specific and relevant information that do not jeopardise our national security interests. In our written submission we've already explained that, for example, we can neither confirm nor deny the existence of intercepted communications. Similarly, Canada cannot disclose information provided to it by other countries. So it would be far more productive for the applicant to identify the specific information sought rather than its form or source. But until the applicant formulates a request that would allow states to cooperate voluntarily, an application for a compulsory order is unjustifiable. Mr. President, members of the Tribunal, before concluding I would like to correct an assertion made by the applicant in his statement -- by the applicant's counsel. The applicant asserted that "Canada states it is a bystander and therefore not subject to the terms of Article 29." This is not the case. What Canada has said on Article 29 is that we recognise and support the power of the Tribunal to issue orders to states for the production of evidence. And that's in paragraph 3 of our written submission, citing Article 29. The applicant has taken Canada's statement that it is a bystander simply out of context. Mr. President, members of the Tribunal, this concludes Canada's oral argument on the application. For all the reasons set out in our written submission as well as those outlined today, the Government of Canada respectfully requests that this application be dismissed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you just tell me --

utterances.speaker: MS. SWORDS
utterances.text: Before closing, if I might make one more comment: We would like to reiterate our commitment to supporting the work of the Tribunal and to provide appropriate assistance to the parties of the Tribunal in the pursuit of international justice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I thank you very much, Ms. Swords. I was going to ask you what are your submissions on the concept of a bystander state.

utterances.speaker: MS. SWORDS
utterances.text: We have made some comments in our oral submission. It's -- sorry, in our written submission, Mr. President. Essentially what we're pointing out is that in the Blaskic decision, when the reference is made to "bystander," it's to states that are not part of the former Republic of Yugoslavia or the Prosecutor or the defendant are in effect bystanders. So the only states that would not be bystanders are those who are part of the former Republic of Yugoslavia. And the point we are making here is that bystanders don't have a direct interest in the specifics of a particular trial, a particular criminal matter. We are watching but we are not the prosecutor and we are not the defendant. Therefore, concerns we may wish to raise with respect to national security are not to be taken lightly. That was the point we are making and it is in paragraph 24 and 25 of our written submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have two questions for you, Ms. Swords. I'll take them separately. First of all, do you have any authority to cite for the proposition that Canada can't produce material given to you by other countries?

utterances.speaker: MS. SWORDS
utterances.text: I believe that in this case, when there are 15 countries who are being asked for information, the authority would be the question of necessity. There is no necessity to be asking for information from -- that may be held by a country with respect -- that is originated by another country when there are so many before the Court. So there really is no necessity, Your Honour, in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the second question -- this is one you may or may not be in a position to answer. It may be my naivety, but I am somewhat surprised that NATO are not represented in this hearing and a motion has been made by the Defence that the very absence amounts to an indication of either willingness to comply or waiver I think was the submission, waiver of the right to oppose the application. Do you have any comments to make on that submission that Mr. Robinson made.

utterances.speaker: MS. SWORDS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I do not. Maybe that is something my colleagues can address tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Swords. We'll next hear from the representative of the Netherlands, that's Mr. Lammers. We'll break for five minutes to allow for an exchange in the seating. --- Break taken at 5.07 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As I said before, we'll now hear submissions now from Mr. Lammers on behalf of the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAMMERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, members of the Chamber, in accordance with paragraph 1 of the Scheduling Order issued by the Trial Chamber on the 22nd September of the year 2004 and Rule 54 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the Netherlands would like to voice certain objections to General Ojdanic for the production of information. General Ojdanic's application -- in General Ojdanic's application the Trial Chamber is requested to order NATO and certain states including the Netherlands to produce three categories of information. First, all recordings, summaries, notes, or text of any intercepted communications, electronic, oral, or written during the period of 1 January through 20 June 1999, to which General Dragoljub Ojdanic was a party. Second, all recordings, summaries, notes or text of any intercepted communications, electronic, oral, or written during that same period originating from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and related to Kosovo in which Mr. Dragoljub Ojdanic was mentioned or referred to in the communication. And third, all correspondence, memoranda, reports, recordings or summaries of any statements made by General Dragoljub Ojdanic during that same period. The Netherlands is fully aware of its obligations under Article 29 of the Tribunal's Statute and Security Council Resolution 827 to comply with any request for assistance or order issued by the Tribunal concerning, inter alia, the production of evidence. Further, the Netherlands has been and remains a firm supporter of the Tribunal and seeks to assist the Tribunal to the greatest extent possible in fulfilling its mandate. Nevertheless, the Netherlands utilising the possible provided for in paragraph 1 of the Scheduling Order to object to the order requested by the applicant. The Netherlands's objections are based on the necessity and relevance on the requested information and on related national security concerns. Should, however, despite its objections, the Trial Chamber decides to grant an order, the Netherlands respectfully submits that it should be reformulated to accommodate these considerable and legitimate objections and that the requested states should be consulted in shaping that order. Mr. President, members of the Chamber, our principal submission is that the Trial Chamber should reject the application. According to Rule 54 bis paragraph (B) 1, the Trial Chamber can reject the application if it determines that: "The documents or information sought are not relevant to any matter at issue in the proceedings before it or are not necessary for a fair determination of any such matter." The Netherlands contends that the application should be rejected on both these grounds. Further, even if the application is deemed to be sufficient to warrant the production of information in general, it does not warrant the overriding of the Netherlands legitimate security concerns. Mr. President, members of the Chamber, the Netherlands is of the opinion that the application fails to establish that the information requested is necessary for a fair determination of any matter at issue in this case, while the Tribunal jurisprudence exists to support the granting of a request for categories of documents unduly broad categories such as those at issue in this case are explicitly prohibited. I refer here to the decision of the Appeals Chamber in the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez. The categories of information requested are impermissibly brought of source material, subject matter, time frame, and place. In fact, the extreme breadth of the request, together with failure of the application to refer to any specific information, indicates that the applicant seeks to engage in a so-called fishing expedition. The applicant is not even certain that such information exists; rather, he seeks to use the power of the Tribunal to ascertain whether this is in fact the case. Such mere speculation is insufficient to justify an order by the Tribunal for the production of information. In addition to its impermissible breadth and the failure of the applicant to establish with any likelihood that such information even exists, the application also fails to satisfy the necessity requirement, as a result of the considerable burden that such an order would place on the requested states. According to the Appeals Chamber, considering whether to grant a request: "Entails the striking of a balance on the need on the one hand of the Tribunal to have the assistance of the states in the collection of evidence for the purpose of prosecuting persons Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law and the need on the other hand to ensure that the obligation upon states to assist the Tribunal in the evidence-collecting process is not unfairly burdensome." Further, in the Blaskic case the Appeals Chamber stated that: "A party cannot request hundreds of documents, particularly when it is evident that the identification, location, and scrutiny of such documents where the relevant national authorities would be overly taxing and not strictly justified by the exigencies of the trial." This is precisely the situation in this case, Mr. President. In this case, given the unparalleled breadth of the request and the large number of states to which it is directed, the burden imposed on the states is considerable. This burden is additionally compounded due to the sensitive nature of certain of the information sought. Access to intelligence information, intercepts in particular, is by necessity extremely limited and thus there are few individuals that can be entrusted with responding to these requests. The imposition manifestly outweighs the limited necessity, if any, established by the application. Moreover, should the requested order be granted, one could expect other defendants to follow suit in the hope that national governments will be ordered to sift through their sensitive intelligence information for any indication of information that might be of use for their case. Such a precedent would magnify the undue burden placed on the states. This in turn would limit their ability to cooperate with the Tribunal requests.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speaker is kindly requested to slow down for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Lammers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAMMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are being asked by the interpreters to speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAMMERS
utterances.text: Slowly? Okay. Such an undue burden is particularly unjustified when it is requested of a state that can be characterised as a concerned bystander. The Appeals Chamber in the Blaskic case ruled that in considering the necessity of an order for production, a distinction between states that are concerned bystanders and states that are directly involved in the conflict is relevant. In this case the Netherlands can be qualified as a concerned bystander to the crimes alleged. I repeat, to the crimes alleged. And thus, the considerable burden requested by the order is all the more unjustified. Finally, the applicant has not established that the requested order is necessary in that the requested information cannot be obtained elsewhere, particularly concerning communications to which the applicant was a party or statements made by the applicant resort to an order to a state seems unnecessary. The applicant is well-suited to know which statements or communications he has made, for various less onerous means exist for bringing this information to the attention of the Trial Chamber, such as calling the parties to the conversations to give evidence. As was stated by the Appeals Chamber in the Blaskic case, the Tribunal should reserve its mandatory compliance powers, I quote: "For cases in which they are really necessary." The Netherlands respectfully argues that due to the unparalleled breadth of the request, its fishing-expedition character, a considerable burden placed on the requested states, many of which can be characterised by standards to the crimes alleged, as well as existence of various less-onerous means for acquiring the information, this is not such a case. Mr. President, members of the Chamber, the requested information is not relevant to any matter at issue. As discussed above, the requested order is very broad in scope and the applicant seeks a wide array of information. This information is of questionable relevance to the applicant's case. The applicant argues that the information requested is directly relevant to show whether he participated in any of the crimes alleged, whether war crimes were reported to him or brought to his attention, and to show his state of mind concerning the events occurring in Kosovo and the prevention and punishment of war crimes. However, in formulating his request, he does not limit it to these issues; rather, he requests copies of all communications during a six-month period to which he was a party or in which he was mentioned or referred to, as well as statements made by him during this period. There is no requirement that any statements have any bearing in the applicant's participation in, knowledge of, or state of mind concerning the crimes alleged. In the applicant's further submission in support of application for orders to NATO and states for production of information, the applicant attempts to remedy this deficiency. He argues that from the information requested it will be possible to show, inter alia, that he did not participate in or have knowledge of the alleged crimes; in other words, that a lack of reference to his participation in or knowledge of the alleged crimes demonstrates that he did not participate in or know about the crimes. However, the extreme breadth of the request and the questionability of proving a negative through this sort of information casts doubt on the relevance of the requested material. As a result, the applicant has failed, in our view, to establish that the requested information is relevant to any matter at issue in the case and his request for an order should therefore be rejected. Disclosure of the requested information raises, in our view, legitimate national security concerns that should be respected. The Tribunal jurisprudence establishes that states are permitted to object to requests for production of information based on national security concerns. This possibility is qualified in Rule 54 bis, paragraph (F). The Netherlands hereby makes such an objection. The Netherlands is aware that a blanket assertion that national security is at stake is insufficient. Rather, it must in Rule 54 bis (F): "identify to the extent possible the basis upon which its national security interests will be prejudiced." In this regard the Netherlands wishes to point out in particular with respect to the first two categories of information sought, the sensitive nature of information relating to the existence of intercepted communications. The very disclosure of such information would cause serious prejudice to national security interests by not only jeopardising the methods and sources utilised to generate that specific information, but also the requested states' ability to gather such information in the future. The arguments are also applicable to the third category of the requested information, to the extent that it includes human intelligence. While provisions can be made to protect the information, risks are nevertheless inherent. The Tribunal should ask states to undergo such inherent risks if it is convinced the applicant has met the heightened burden accompanying this risk. This is all the more so when the Tribunal is addressing disclosure to a state with a history of bona fide cooperation. Mr. President, members of the Chamber, for the reasons stated above, the Trial Chamber should not issue the requested order. If, however, the Trial Chamber decides not to reject the request outright, then the Netherlands respectfully submits that the Trial Chamber should narrow the scope of any order granted. As discussed above, the requested order is impermissibly broad. Any order granted should significantly reduce the breadth of the request, at a minimum to include only information that has a bearing on the applicant's participation in, knowledge of, or state of mind concerning the crimes alleged. Also excluded should be information which the applicant could acquire from other sources and information, disclosure of which would jeopardise the requested state's national security. In this regard, any order would need to provide for appropriate arrangements to protect requested state's national security interests, including but not limited to the possibility to submit the information in redacted form; I refer to Rule 54 bis (F) (ii) and (G) and (I), and the possibility to offer protection similar to that supplied by the Prosecutor on a confidential basis under Rule 70. It is respectfully argued that should the Chamber decide to issue such an order it consult requested states concerning modalities to alleviate their concerns. Mr. President, members of the Chamber, in conclusion, for the reasons just given, the Netherlands respectfully submits that the order should not be granted. Specifically, the information sought is not necessary or demonstrably relevant and the Netherlands, a bystander state to the crimes alleged with a history of bona fide cooperation, has a legitimate national security concerns with the requested order. In the alternative, should the Trial Chamber should decide to issue an order, it should narrow it to only include information relevant to the applicant's participation in, knowledge of or state of mind concerning the crimes. Further, the applicant should be required to specify the communications and statements of which he would like copies. Also excluded should be information which the applicant could acquire from other sources and the disclosure of which would jeopardise the requested state's national security. Finally, any such order would need to provide for appropriate arrangements to protect the requested state's national security interests, with regard to any information that was ordered to be produced, including the possibility to offer protections similar to those contained in Rule 70. Mr. President, Members of the Chamber, thank you for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lammers. I'd just like to raise one question, and again I return to this concept of the concerned bystander, as distinct from a state more directly affected, the states located on the territory of the former Yugoslavia. It would not be correct that there is any legal consequence to be drawn from this distinction. The Appeals Chamber in Blaskic itself made it clear that the distinction only has a practical consequence in that states of the former Yugoslavia are more likely to be required to cooperate in the ways envisaged in Article 29. I raise it because it's not clear to me from the submissions that were made by Canada, and now by you, whether that is clearly understood because I somehow have the impression that you seem to be indicating that there is a different legal regime for a concerned bystander, and that is not the case at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAMMERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your permission, the notion that a bystander state as we understand is -- we were a belligerent party in Kosovo, we don't deny that. And in that sense we were not a bystanding state, so to say. What we mean by bystanding state here is we were not active on the ground. We were not involved in things which occurred on the ground.
