We were not a bystanding state in things that happened on the ground and which are here -- the alleged crimes that are here at issue at the moment. And in that sense we believe that we are -- not a bystanding state. Thank you very much. And we were not directly concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In other words, Mr. Lammers, even if you are a bystanding state and you have relevant information and the other requirements of Rule 54 bis are met, then you are required to produce it; that's my understanding of Blaskic. The distinction only has a practical consequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAMMERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we will certainly look into the possibility to see whether we have information which we will be able to produce, but we say already now that being in the position of a bystanding state, the chance may be not be great, that we will not be able to provide the information that you are looking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think you are now addressing the practicality of it, yes. I will just ask other speakers to address that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I say on a separate matter that so far I have not been particularly assisted by the submissions in relation to national security interests. It's universally known nowadays that communications are intercepted. There are widespread public debates to the use of which intercepted communications should be put. And if that's the only argument parties have about the matter, there's little point in making it. If, however, there's something more substantial to this point, then I would be interested in hearing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAMMERS
utterances.text: With your permission, I have been informed that -- well, the system of recording the information, certainly at the time which we have in view here, in 1999, for the Netherlands is complex -- is a complex situation. And we don't dispose of the technologically advanced systems of recording which other states may dispose of, certainly not at the time which we have in mind at the moment. Moreover, it's not only the question of finding information, it's also the question of scrutinising the material. And as we have already outlined in our earlier speech, there are only a few individuals at the disposal of the Netherlands which are entrusted with responding to these requests --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I took that point, Mr. Lammers. I understood that. But as Ms. Swords pointed out, it's not the method that matters here, it's the product. And really, how that material is obtained will not be the concern of any order that's made here. The order, if it's made, will simply be related to the product of the exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAMMERS
utterances.text: I understand that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lammers. Next on the list is the United Kingdom. Professor Greenwood.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREENWOOD
utterances.text: I'm quite happy to start now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREENWOOD
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, members of the Court, I have the pleasure and privilege of appearing on behalf of the United Kingdom before you today. The United Kingdom has always been very keen to cooperate with the Tribunal and indeed has gone to the greatest possible lengths to do, but we strongly oppose the submission that has been made by counsel for the Defence in the present proceedings. Mr. President, before I turn to the substance of my own submissions, I wonder if I might respond briefly to the question that My Lord Bonomy asked of Ms. Swords in the position of NATO. Now, obviously I am not instructed here on behalf of NATO; I am instructed on behalf of the United Kingdom, and I am sure that attempts will be made over the course of the recess to contact counsel for NATO or to contact those who are entitled to speak on behalf of her. But I wonder if I might make this point: NATO has no methods of its own for acquiring information. It has no intelligence of its own. It has no communications interception facilities of its own. Any information covered by the present request which might be in the possession of NATO - and I stress, might be in the possession of NATO - can therefore only have come from one of the member states. The Defence has made applications against all of the member states of NATO, although it has now withdrawn those requests in respect of some of the members. So just as my learned friend, counsel for Canada, made the point to the Court that where a state has information which has been communicated to it from another state, the appropriate course for the Defence is to seek that information from the source state. That is the way -- that is the appropriate way to apply Rule 54 bis. That same principle must hold good, we submit, in respect of NATO. It is from the states that that information should be sought, if it is to be sought at all. I merely put that forward today because I do not wish it to be thought that by not being here on the present occasion, NATO is in some way being disrespectful to the Tribunal or that somehow there has been any waiver of the objections that are being taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: May I say, Professor Greenwood, I am not surprised at all by the explanation you give and I have a fair deal of sympathy with the submission you make about seeking material, first of all, from the originating source. But is there any authority for the proposition you make, that it should be sought from the originating source rather than the secondary source?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREENWOOD
utterances.text: Well, My Lord, to the best of my knowledge there is no direct authority in the Tribunal on this point, although we will endeavour to research it overnight. But, My Lord, in my submission, it does follow a matter of common sense and logic from the way Rule 54 bis is structured, and it's particularly germane to the facts of this case. This will touch on a point I want to deal with later in my submissions, but what the Defence is seeking to do here is not to get hold of a specific piece of information. There's no smoking gun, if one can use that term, that they are chasing. What they are seeking to do is to demonstrate a negative to the Tribunal. They are seeking to establish from a variety of conversations, as I will endeavour to show, quite a considerable variety that General Ojdanic did not have the mens rea for the offences charged, did not have the necessary knowledge. Now, if that is the purpose for which the information is sought, then two things immediately become very important. The first is the methodology by which the information is obtained, because that goes to the question of its reliability. And that, of course, is information which is only likely to reside with the state that is the source of the information. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Secondly, if you are seeking to prove a negative, it really doesn't help you very much to show that a particular issue was not mentioned in the course of the five, ten, 15, 50 conversations of which you have intercepts. You've got to show that those intercepts are reasonably comprehensive, and there are unlikely to have been other conversations in which the relevant matter might have been mentioned or the incriminating sentences might have been spoken. So that question of whether the intelligence material is comprehensive is likely something that is able to be answered by the state that acquired that in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One answer to that would be to specify the occasions which would then lead the Court here, perhaps, to see the relevance of these and possibly the necessity of obtaining that material from that source.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREENWOOD
utterances.text: Well, My Lord, that may be the case, but in my respectful submission that entire dialogue is one that can be had and has to be had, if it is going to be had at all, with the state that is the supposed source of the intercepts. It cannot meet criteria of necessity to go a secondary or tertiary party and ask them what someone else has given them, when you can go to the original source of the information and get the answer in an unadulterated form from that source. So the best-evidence rule must be applicable here. You go to the state that is most likely to be able to give you that information. And in the presence case, that is precisely what the Defence has done. It has made applications against all of the NATO member states. So there cannot be, in those circumstances, any necessity for an order against NATO. My lords, unless I can assist you further with that particular point, let me move, if I may, to the main substance of my submissions. Now, the United Kingdom made written submissions in response to the Defence application some 20 months ago in February 2003. There have of course been a number of developments since that time. There has been Prosecution disclosure, we understand, under Rule 66 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. There have been further submissions by Defence counsel in June 2003. So to have a hearing at this stage is apposite. It is necessary to revisit the arguments that were made in writing nearly two years ago. But we say that on closer inspection nothing has changed at all. The Defence has done nothing during the nearly two years that it has had to refine its request in any way and all the objections which the United Kingdom has made in our written submissions, still apply today. I don't propose to repeat them to the Tribunal; that would obviously be unnecessary, but I want to make clear that the fact that I am not repeating them does not in any way mean we are not departing from them. What I wish to do is concentrate on the submissions the Defence has made both in its brief June 2003 and orally this afternoon. Now, we say that the first and perhaps in many ways the most important consideration is this: The Defence has wholly failed to follow the procedure laid down in Rule 54 bis for making an application of this kind. Rule 54 bis was designed to give effect to the principles initially set out by the Appeals Chamber in the Blaskic decision. One of those principles was summarised by the Blaskic Chamber in these terms: "In the final analysis, the Tribunal may discharge its functions only if it can count on the bona fide assistance and cooperation of sovereign states. It is therefore to be regarded as sound policy for the Prosecutor as well as Defence counsel first to seek through cooperative means the assistance of states and only if they decline to lend support, then to request a Judge or Trial Chamber to have recourse to the mandatory action provided for in Article 29 of the Statute." And it's for that reason that Rule 54 bis requires the Defence to show that it has taken reasonable steps to secure cooperation, that it has really tried to exhaust the cooperative process before seeking to go down the mandatory road. Now, the Defence says in its application to this Tribunal that General Ojdanic has: "gone to great lengths in this regard, great lengths." Well, it is worth looking at what really happened and contrasting it with that sentence. First of all, on the 17th of May, 2002, the Defence wrote to the United Kingdom, and as we understand to other states here, in terms which are similar to though not identical to the request. That letter was forwarded on the 20th of June, 2002, by the Tribunal to the Foreign and Commonwealth Office in London. And on the 26th of June, the Foreign and Commonwealth office received that letter and acknowledged its receipt. On the 26th of July, 2002, the United Kingdom replied in these terms to the Defence. It's at page 7.101 of the record. "Your letter sets out three very broad categories of material, copies of which you request should be disclosed to you. In order to assist us in considering your request, it would be helpful if you were able to specify in as much further detail as possible the material to which your request relates." Now, Mr. President, that we say is very far from being a negative response. It certainly is not declining to assist the Defence. The Defence response is said to have been an e-mail which appears at 7.100 of the record, which we are told was sent to the Foreign Office on the 5th of September, 2002. But the first that the British government heard of it was when the present application was made. We never received the e-mail and, indeed, we wrote to the Defence in January of 2003 to say that we had never received the e-mail referred to in their application. But although it was not received, the e-mail is worth looking at because it tells us a lot about what this present application is and how the Defence has gone about its duty of cooperation under Rule 54 bis. If I just quote the relevant passages of it to the Tribunal. This is an e-mail from Mr. Peter Robinson to Mr. McDuff [phoen] of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office who was the signatory of the letter of 26 July 2002: "In 1999, leading up to and during the war in Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Professor, Greenwood, you're being asked to slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREENWOOD
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. It's because I'm reading. I'll speak more slowly. "In 1999, leading up to and during the war in Kosovo, intelligence agencies of several governments intercepted communications of persons within the military and civilian command structure of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. We are requesting that your government search its files and disclose to us those communications, one, in which General Ojdanic was a participant; or two, in which General Ojdanic was mentioned. This need only be for the six-month period from January to June 1999. That seems very specific to me," Mr. Robinson says. "You can contact any agency which participates in this kind of intelligence gathering and ask them to look for these communications. Perhaps a word search using the word 'Ojdanic' would be a good start. "Our third request is for memoranda or other reports that relate to statements by or about General Ojdanic. This is one step removed from an intercepted communication. Here, we are seeking disclosure of what people in your government reported General Ojdanic as saying or what others said about him during this six-month period." Then there's a reference to the military attache, Colonel Crossland [phoen], in Belgrade. "So we are asking you to canvass any agency of your government involved in intelligence, military, or diplomatic affairs and look for any reports, memoranda, et cetera," -- one wonders what the word et cetera might cover, given what's already gone in -- "in which General Ojdanic is mentioned during the limited period of the first six months of 1999. I hope this response is helpful to you and we look forward to your cooperation." Now, there is incidentally nothing in the record here to indicate the date on which that e-mail was sent, which machine it was sent from, what e-mail system was used to send it, or who was the e-mail addressee, although the e-mail of Mr. McDuff is given on his letter of the 26th of July, as is his telephone number. Now after that, complete silence. There is not a word from the Defence. They don't follow up to find out why they've had no response to the e-mail. They don't telephone Mr. McDuff, they don't write, they don't send another e-mail. Nothing happens at all. Even after the 13th of January, 2003, when the Defence will have received a letter from the British government saying that that e-mail had not been received, there is still no follow-up. And in the nearly two years since then, not a word. And in his submissions this afternoon, Mr. Robinson said that the governments have made no effort to contact the Defence during the two years since they were originally contacted. Let me turn that around. What effort has the Defence made? The burden is on the Defence to meet the requirements of Rule 54 bis. What steps has the Defence taken? The answer is very simple: It hasn't taken any. And it's particularly significant, because as we understand it during that two-year period, although I'm not in a position to say exactly when, Prosecution disclosure was made under Rule 66. Now, that would have given the Defence quite a considerable idea of, first of all, of what was the case it had to meet; secondly, what information the Prosecution was going to deploy against it; and thirdly, what meetings, exchanges of correspondence, telephone calls might be part of the evidence in the Prosecution case. Now, the Defence had adverted to that in the application they made. If members of the Tribunal will look at page 7.122 of the record, paragraph 10 of the application, footnote 9, they'll find this sentence: "General Ojdanic envisages this as being the first request for binding orders. The second request covering a wider range of materials will be made once disclosure by the Prosecutor has been completed so that General Ojdanic will be in a position to be as specific as possible with respect to those materials." Now, Mr. President, leaving aside the fact that it refers to an even wider request rather than a more specific one, a matter I'll come back to in a moment, there are two points that are clear from that footnote. First of all, it recognises the significance of Prosecution disclosure for the work of the Defence; yet not a word from the Defence since Prosecution disclosure has occurred. And secondly, that footnote surely indicates, if one needed any further evidence of it, that the Defence has given up on any idea of cooperation with the states. There's no suggestion here that after Prosecution disclosure the Defence is going to make another -- write another letter and invite a cooperative response from the states. No, it's envisioning going straight back to the Tribunal for a second binding order. That, we say, is plainly not what Rule 54 bis requires. And as I say, it is worth recalling the fact that the burden is on the Defence as the party making this application to show that it has met all the requirements of the rules. The Blaskic case, albeit that it was decided before Rule 54 bis was adopted, nevertheless makes quite clear what in the spirit of this rule is required. In the cooperative process, the party seeking evidence, be it the Prosecutor or the Defence, is required to go the extra mile. Well, far from going the extra mile and seeking cooperation, the Defence in the present case seems to have been reluctant to even put its foot on the road. It has taken no active steps in cooperation at all, other than a rather bland suggestion that perhaps a word search using the word "Ojdanic" would be a good place to start. As I will endeavour to show it wouldn't have been a particularly useful place to start at all. Now, Mr. President, it's common ground between the Defence and ourselves that this is not a case in which the Tribunal should be making new law, it's a case for applying existing principles and applying them fairly. The jurisprudence of the Tribunal and this language of Rule 54 bis makes clear what those main principles are. First of all, there is no scope for a fishing expedition. What the Defence must do is request specific information or documents, detailed as far as possible and limited in number -- a specific requirement in the Appeals Chamber's decision in Blaskic. But if one looks at this request, it's about as far from those principles as it would be possible to imagine: "All intercepts of any communication to which General Ojdanic was a party during a period of six months." And although Mr. Robinson concentrated on the word "intercepts," his request is actually broader than that. He doesn't just want primary intercepts, he wants all notes, summaries, records of such intercepts as well; assessments made on the basis of those intercepts. What would be involved is potentially - indeed, on the face of the request, because the request makes great play of the fact that there was a great deal of intelligence gathering going on - is potentially thousands and thousands of documents and pieces of information. And with respect to my learned friend Mr. Robinson, I fear he rather misquoted the Kordic decision to Your Lordships this afternoon because he suggested that that decision expressly envisaged hundreds of documents being revealed. So far as I can see, it does the exact opposite. At paragraph 34, subparagraph 3 of the Kordic decision it summarises the existing law and in particular the Blaskic ruling, that a binding order for the production of documents must: "Not be unduly onerous. As already referred to above, a party cannot request hundreds of documents, particularly when it is evident that the identification, location and scrutiny of such documents by the relevant national authorities would be overly taxing and not strictly justified by the exigencies of the trial." Mr. President, I've got about another ten minutes of submissions. I don't know whether you would like me to try and finish this evening or whether you would prefer me to resume tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, try to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREENWOOD
utterances.text: I shall endeavour to do so. Now, there has been no attempt by the Defence to be more specific than simply seeking this broad range of intercepts of any meeting where General Ojdanic was a participant, any conversation in which he took part. And yet General Ojdanic must know perfectly well what were the main meetings that he attended during that period. It simply isn't good enough for counsel for the Defence to say that he doesn't remember every telephone conversation he had. Well, one wouldn't expect that. But I would imagine that he does remember every major meeting that he went to during that period, every conversation he had with the president or a senior member of the government. And yet nothing which narrows down the field, nothing which enables people to pinpoint documents more readily has been offered. Moreover, the second limb of the request seeks all intercepts, summaries, records in which General Ojdanic is mentioned, even though he wasn't a party to the conversation and wasn't present. And the third limb seeks all correspondence, memoranda, reports, recordings, or summaries of any statements made by General Ojdanic during this period to: "Any representative of your organisation, including sources of information working on your behalf." Now, we say that comes nowhere near the level of specificity required by the Appeals Chamber in Blaskic and Kordic or the level of specificity required by Rule 54 bis. It is a classic instance of a fishing expedition. What the Defence wish to do is they want leave to troll through the records of the intelligence services, the armed forces, the foreign ministries, the embassies, and the other agencies of originally 25 states; now we're narrowed down to 12. In the Delalic case, Judge Hunt, to whom my learned friend Ms. Swords referred earlier, defined a fishing expedition in these terms: "One where the party that had no evidence that fish of a particular kind were in the pool, but wanted to drag the pool to find whether there were any such fish there or not." Well, in response to your question, Mr. President, Mr. Robinson quite candidly admitted that there was always an element of fishing in any application for disclosure of documents. What characterised his request, he said, is that it was effectively a licensed form of fishing. He got his certificate, he could dip his rod into the pond. He's not seeking to dip a rod into the pond. He's seeking to take an ocean-going trawler out to sea with a dragnet as fine as possible and drag it up and down the oceans until he finds something that looks interesting. Nor is he Captain Ahab searching for the white whale. He doesn't have one particular piece of information, one particular fish in mind. He's after whatever fish can be found. Keep in mind also, Mr. President, that footnote that I read out from that application for disclosure. The footnote envisages a second request at a later stage. It's not too difficult to contemplate what that's going to be. It's going to be a request for, Defence having already sought intercepts of any conversations or meetings of which General Ojdanic was a party or where he was mentioned, the next request is going to be for everything where he isn't mentioned because it's the fact that he isn't mentioned or the fact that his name didn't come up which is significant in showing that he was involved. That's what lies as the next step down this particular line. So we say it doesn't come near to meeting the specificity requirement. What about the requirement that the request be not unduly burdensome? Well, the Defence has claimed that no state has shown why the request would be unduly burdensome in this case. That's an expressed statement in their June 2003 submissions. Well, that quite simply is not the case. In paragraphs 26 to 30 of the United Kingdom's written submissions, we did indeed set out why the request would be unduly burdensome. The short answer is that quite apart from the sheer volume of material which is potentially covered by a request as broad as this, the material which would have to be searched in order to find this information is held in the United Kingdom by several different departments or agencies. It's not gathered in one place. It is by no means, all of it, available in electronic form. That rather facile suggestion that a word search with the word Ojdanic is a good place to start is patently not going to produce the answer that the Defence want. The Defence wants material which is often held only in written form, not held electronically. Indeed, that I suppose is recognised in fairness in the e-mail of September of 2002 by the way in which it says that a word search might be a good place to start. Where would one go, one asks, after that start has been made? And the failure to be specific is a large part of the problem here. Even where the defendant could easily have been more specific, for example by listing the meetings which General Ojdanic attended, they haven't done so. It's perfectly apparent that the burden in this case is going to fall entirely on the states. The Defence really doesn't wish to be involved in facilitating that task at all. Mr. President, two other points briefly, if I may, in conclusion. The first concerns the requirement of relevance and necessity that the information sought must be relevant to the trial and its disclosure must be necessary for the trial, the requirements set out in the Kordic case and in Rule 54 bis. We respectfully endorse the submission made earlier by counsel for the Government of Canada that Kordic does not preclude states from raising this issue, though of course the question of whether information is relevant or necessary falls to be determined by the Chamber. It's not something on which the states can have the last word. And the United Kingdom has certainly not suggested that it can. But the problem here is that when the dragnet has been cast as wide as it has, it's almost impossible to say what is going to be relevant or whether its disclosure is going to be necessary. And the submission made by the Defence both in their June brief and in their speech this afternoon that of course anything might be relevant, if you know enough about the case, in showing that General Ojdanic didn't have the necessary knowledge, didn't have the necessary mental state. That's a submission which really proves too much. Far from showing that the material sought is indeed necessary, it shows that the Defence wants to troll through whatever it can get its hands on in order to try and identify something relevant and something necessary in the middle. The Defence of course is not required in a criminal trial to prove a negative. The burden is on the Prosecution to prove that General Ojdanic committed the offences charged with the necessary mental element. The Defence is not required to prove his innocence. And therefore seeking a vast volume of material like this really cannot meet the requirement of relevance and necessity. Lastly, Mr. President, a brief word bearing in mind My Lord Lord Bonomy's comments a moment ago about the national security concerns. Let me make it clear that the United Kingdom is not seeking a blanket national security exception. But the Blaskic case does make clear that national security concerns of states are relevant considerations to be taken into account and the procedure in Rule 54 bis was fashioned precisely to enable that to be done, to enable a security issue to be raised about certain information. But in the present case, it's almost impossible to do that. One cannot conduct that exercise with a request in terms as broad as this. Now, that there are going to be security concerns we say is perfectly obvious. Of course it is known that communications are intercepted. But that doesn't -- that's not the point at all. The question is the security significance of a particular conversation having been intercepted at a particular time; the method by which it was intercepted, which may be of considerable relevance to its reliability and therefore to the strength that the Defence, the weight the Defence is seeking to place upon it. And take also the human intelligence element. The third part of the request is perhaps rather coyly drafted, but that reference to "sources acting on your behalf" is plainly intended to include informants and human intelligence sources. And that potentially raises a vast security concern about the identification of somebody whose life may be put at risk, the identification of methods of intelligence gathering, which might put people's lives at risk in the future. Now, I take My Lord Lord Bonomy's point that he's not been greatly assisted by the fact we haven't been able to go into detail about the national security concerns. The problem is the breadth of the request is such that it's extremely difficult for the states to pinpoint which pieces of information might raise the concern. That is why the whole purpose of Rule 54 bis is, we say, being subverted by this application. Rule 54 bis permits a balancing of security interests with against the necessity of having information for a trial. You cannot achieve that balance with a request as broad-brush as this. That is why our respectful submission is that this application should be dismissed. We do not, with respect, feel that the order can be refashioned on the hoof in a way which might meet our concerns. What we would call on the Defence to do is what it should have done in the first place: to go through the Rule 54 bis initially by entering into a dialogue with the states concerned. That is the only way this matter can be approached. Now, Your Honour, I apologise for having trespassed beyond the 6.00 finishing time. Unless I can assist the members of the Tribunal in any way, that concludes the submissions for the United Kingdom.
